superficial: A blackboard full to the edges. A long equation in round handwriting that stops halfway; several lines have dry red strokes through them, in another hand. Beside it, the broken chalk.
In a corner, in small letters: "If it leaves through the Mouth, add. If it leaves through the Well, subtract. DO NOT forget the delay of the journey."
profunda: Now you know what is missing: the reckoning for the Counterweight's clock. It depends on the route it takes to Scar.
However long the trip takes, at the rate time runs wherever it passes, has to be subtracted from the machine's clock.

superficial: "Day 1,300 in here. Out there, 260. It is finished. We have not tested it: testing it means putting it in place of the engine."
"It is a replacement engine. It does not fix the debt: it pays it, little by little, instead of letting it be collected all at once."
"If you read this, don't hurry: take it to the machine on Scar. It goes where the old engine goes."
profunda: One more page, folded under the others: "There is a new call. A young system, very far away, has opened a Mouth and is calling ours."
"They don't know what they are doing. Neither did we."
On the back of the last sheet, underlined: “It has nothing to run on. What it lacks he has, in the Chamber. Each of us keeps one half.”

superficial: "I said it out loud three times. There is a limit: every crossing through a Gate pulls the clocks a little further apart, and one day the network cannot hold."
"They asked me for figures. I brought them. They asked me not to repeat them."
At the end of the last page, pressed harder: "It is too late to warn anyone. Whatever leaves this place will arrive late."
profunda: Under the last figure, in another hand, round: “Pay it, yes. But first you need something to pay with.” It is the scientist's hand.
They wanted the same thing, that there be time for everyone; they only argued over the road.

superficial: An envelope with the Council's seal, carefully opened and closed again. Inside, a single sheet:

"For the good of the network and of all who depend on it, the conclusions of the Route 7 group will not leave this place. No measurements will be sent. No warnings will be given. Any communication will first pass through the Council."
The signature is smudged, as if someone had run a thumb over it many times.

A room without a roof, with two beds pushed against each other. In one, the blankets are rumpled and there is the hollow of a head on the pillow. The other is made up with care, without a crease: nobody has slept in it for a long time.
Between the two, a burned-down candle and two cups, side by side.
On its stand, between two supports, a device the size of an arm: brass rings nested one inside another, with a small clock at the centre.
On its base, engraved, a diamond with a dot inside. It is finished. It has not a single mark of use.
profunda: You bring your hand close: something pushes outward, as if the air weighed less around it. The clock at the centre runs faster than yours.
It is not an engine that pulls at the debt: it is something that opposes it, like the opposite of gravity.

superficial: Two crossed rings, dark, around a frozen slab. On it, standing under the frost, someone with a diamond and a dot on the chest: they have been there a long time.
On the edge of the slab, by hand, a single word: “Wait”.
Shelves of tape boxes, labelled by cycle. On the wall, two clocks: "Inside" and "Outside". The inside one turns five times for every turn of the outside one.
On the table, a column of figures climbing and climbing: "How long a message from outside takes to arrive here. How long one of ours takes to leave." At the bottom, underlined: "Always late."
A slate cabinet with five dials; a red light that no longer blinks. On the wall, strips of paper pinned up: messages received, each with two dates, the one outside and the one in here.
The last one: "Council to Route 7. Keep silent. The Gates remain open." Under it, a reply written by hand and never sent: "Close them."
A table set for two. One cup upright; the other knocked over, with the dried stain around it. Nobody picked it up.
In the cupboard the jars are almost empty and lined up from fullest to emptiest, as if someone had counted the days that were left.
A whole wall of tally marks, in fives. At the top, "here": the count does not fit and runs on along the edge of the wall. Below, in red, "outside": a few months.
At the end of the "here" row, one mark shorter than the rest, as if whoever made it had tired halfway through.
Beds of dry soil with very long stalks, all leaning towards the centre of the cavity, towards the seed, as if it were the sun.
In the growth notebook, the last entry: "They no longer grow towards the lamps. They grow towards that. We turned the lamps off to see if they would stop. They don't."
Beside the dark Gate, a post of black stone with a twelve-hour face. One hand runs fast; the other stands still at an hour that is not the hour.
Carved in the base: "It keeps the time inside. Inside, five turns for every one outside." On its side, two brass wheels: minutes and seconds.
Above, an amber light blinks, like someone knocking at a door nobody opens.
Under the two rings, standing before a slab of ice, someone waits covered in frost. A rhombus with a dot inside is carved in the slab; the same sign glows, very faintly, on their chest.
Beside it, a brass wheel and four unlit lights. On the edge, by hand: "Slowly. One turn, then wait for the frost to give. If you force it, it closes."
The frost falls from her suit in flakes. She sits on the edge of the bed, slowly, like someone who does not yet trust her knees.
"What day is it in here? And outside?..." She thinks about it. "No, never mind. The two clocks would not tell me the same thing any more."
"You came in through the Gate, from outside. So someone knew how to set it right. Good."
"When I feel better, I will go and see if he is all right. I hope the cold kept me for something."
She listens with her hands together on her knees. When you tell her he is alive, the sign on her chest brightens a little.
"Alive. Good." A long pause. "Does he sleep? Does he eat anything?... Don't answer if you don't know."
"Still counting, then. Counter."
"When I feel better, I will go and see if he is all right. Don't warn him: he would want to tidy the table first."
She looks at what you carry before she looks at you. She leans on the bed so as not to stand up.
"You are carrying it. It weighs more than it seems, and not because of the brass."
"Take it to him. He will know where it fits. And don't tell him what it costs: he knows better than anyone."
"When I feel better, I will go and see if he is all right. Don't you rush: the count is not paid in a hurry."
